summary: A note on two new features of the Multics network software. One is case mapping, activated by typing MAP, which helps users on upper-case-only terminals. It describes typing conventions for letters and some symbols. The other new feature is also described.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 411 describes two changes to Multics network software. One translated input from uppercase-only terminals, and the other handled small data allocations with fewer interruptions.

questions: how did multics handle uppercase-only terminals
what did the map command do
how did multics improve handling of small allocations
subtitle: Two Multics network software changes for terminals and transfers

tldr.problem: Uppercase-only terminals had difficulty supplying the lowercase input Multics expected, and small allocations caused pauses and processing overhead.
tldr.mechanism: Multics added case-mapping conventions and code to process allocation messages during interrupts without waking the Network Daemon.
tldr.outcome: The note reports improved access for limited terminals and better response when output used small allocations.

today: RFC 411 describes two recently installed features in Multics network software. The note explains their intended behavior and the reported response improvement.

sections.title: Case Mapping for Uppercase-Only Terminals
sections.content:
A user could type MAP after the Multics load message to activate case-mapping software. The software converted alphabetic input to lowercase, except where the stated typing conventions indicated otherwise, and used escape sequences for several characters that the terminal could not type directly.

Typing HELP before login in response to a login-incorrect message also activated the mapping behavior and printed login information.
sections.plainLanguage: Typing MAP enabled conventions for entering the lowercase letters and special characters Multics expected. HELP before login could also activate the feature and show login instructions.

sections.title: Handling Small Allocations
sections.content:
When a destination system offered small allocations, output could pause often and the Multics Network Daemon could be woken repeatedly to process ALL control messages. The new interrupt-time code processed those messages and sent the next group of bytes without waking the daemon.

The RFC reports better response under the new scheme and notes that allocation messages accounted for about 75% of Multics control-message processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Small allocations used to cause frequent pauses and wake-ups. New code handled each allocation as part of interrupt processing, reducing the need to wake the daemon.

sections.title: The Two Features Together
sections.content: The RFC presents case mapping and allocation handling as separate improvements to Multics network software. One concerns how users enter characters; the other concerns how the system processes groups of outgoing data when the receiving system grants small allocations.
sections.plainLanguage: One change helped users type on limited keyboards. The other helped Multics send output more smoothly to systems with small allocations.
